hints: Focus on how reactive the starting organic molecule is, especially the electron rich C=C double bond in ethene.
Remember the bromine water test for an alkene, the orange colour disappears instantly in the cold with no heating or catalyst.
Contrast that instant electrophilic addition with the other three reactions, which all need strong heating, concentrated acid or high pressure to work.
walkthrough:
**Identify the type of each reaction**

Think like a chemist and sort them by family. A and B are additions to ethene, C is dehydration of ethanol, D is substitution of ethanol to make a bromoalkane.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Br}_2$$

**Recall the conditions needed for B, C and D**

These three all have high activation energy. Hydration of ethene needs steam, about 300 degrees C and a phosphoric acid catalyst. Dehydration of ethanol needs hot concentrated sulfuric acid. Substitution with $\text{HBr}$ needs heating under reflux.

**Spot the reaction that needs no heating**

Electrophilic addition of bromine to the double bond is very fast at 20 degrees C. The pi electrons attack $\text{Br}_2$ immediately, so the brown colour vanishes quickly in the cold. That is why this one is different from the rest.

options.A: Correct. Electrophilic addition of $\text{Br}_2$ to ethene is rapid at room temperature with no catalyst or heating. The pi bond is electron rich and readily polarises $\text{Br}_2$, so $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{Br}_2$ forms quickly.
options.B: False. Hydration of ethene to ethanol needs harsh conditions, typically steam at about 300 degrees C, about 60 atm pressure and a concentrated $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ catalyst. It does not happen quickly at 20 degrees C.
options.C: False. Dehydration of ethanol to ethene is an elimination that needs hot concentrated sulfuric or phosphoric acid, around 170 degrees C. Students sometimes reverse B and C, but both need heating.
options.D: False. Substitution of the $\text{OH}$ group by $\text{Br}$ using $\text{HBr}$ is slow at room temperature for a primary alcohol. It requires heating under reflux to break the strong C-O bond and drive the reaction.
